extracted.intended_audience: theoretical computer scientists, researchers in complexity theory, and an informed scientific audience interested in P vs NP
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating claimed P vs NP proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and community norms for assessing and responding to a claimed major proof in theoretical computer science (here, a claimed proof that P != NP). Covers technical, procedural, and community-evidence criteria that determine whether a claimed proof is credible, fixable, or publishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make drafts public for broad review
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should make drafts available publicly for rapid, broad, and comprehensive community review rather than limiting circulation to journals or a few experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple commenters argue that public posting leverages the internet for the quickest and sharpest review; withholding drafts (sending only to journals) 'doesn't improve the acceptability' and slows community scrutiny. Counterpoints note authors may prefer formal journal review for 'due process'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-reviewed journal publication and standing period
rubrics_metrics.description: For prizes such as the Clay Millennium problems, a proof must be published in a peer-reviewed journal and stand unrefuted for a specified period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post cites Clay's requirement that proofs of Millennium Problems 'be published in a peer reviewed journal and stand for two years.' This is a procedural criterion for final acceptance of major results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a full, detailed draft (complete technical details)
rubrics_metrics.description: A credible major proof should include a full draft containing all details (not just high-level ideas); substantial length (e.g., 200–300 pages) may be necessary as details are expanded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes the author's 'full' draft is growing as details are added (perhaps 200–300 pages). Commenters warn that long proofs can hide subtle fatal errors and require extensive scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make critical parts falsifiable and give rigorous definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Key claims and critical components of the argument must be stated in a falsifiable, precise way with clear definitions (e.g., of 'partial assignment' or topology used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters criticize versions that 'make a falsifiable statement in this critical part of the proof' and urge formal definitions so objections and checks can be unambiguously applied. Lack of such precision makes community verification difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer machine-checked proofs where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine-checked formalization offers near-certain correctness and dramatically reduces the human inspection burden, making acceptance effectively instant once the statement and definitions are formalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One comment notes that a machine-checked proof would give 'nearly instant acceptance' because only definitions and the statement need human inspection; however, formalizing a very long informal proof is acknowledged as a major effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond constructively to raised issues and revise transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should address known objections, clarify concepts, and release revised manuscripts that document fixes and simplifications transparently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post and comments note the author claimed to have 'fixed all the issues' and to have obtained 'simpler proofs of several claims'; transparent revision and communication of what was fixed helps community confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely resolution and community interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary claims should be resolved in a timely manner; the community and claimant share an interest in getting closure quickly so effort can be focused productively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post asks how long a major claim should remain unresolved and suggests both the claimant and community benefit from prompt resolution. Excessively long unresolved claims create prolonged distraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid argument strategies that are provably inapplicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on classes of arguments that the community has identified as incapable of resolving the question (e.g., certain finite-model-theory or 'solution-space geometry' approaches that have been shown to fail in key ways).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argued the paper had fatal misapplications (finite model theory) and that some general argument classes cannot settle P vs NP; such methodological errors are fatal rather than minor technicalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against 'SAT0' and similar mapping/perspective pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure arguments are robust to simple transformations and reductions (e.g., mappings that produce 'SAT0' or permute variables), which can show that claimed structural properties don't imply hardness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple comments outline how mapping SAT to problems like 'SAT0' (trivial to solve) via permutations or encodings preserves solution-space features while making the decision easy, undermining arguments that rely solely on solution-space complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sure the methodology addresses ensemble/distribution-level properties if reliant on random-instance behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proof strategy uses properties of random k-SAT or average-case phenomena, it must clearly connect those distributional properties to worst-case complexity or demonstrate why distributional structure precludes membership in P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments note pointwise (single-instance) solution-space arguments are unlikely to succeed; a successful approach would need to reason about the set/ensemble of instances (moduli space) or otherwise show how random-instance structure yields provable worst-case hardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and defend why an algorithm cannot exploit the same structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof must argue convincingly that no polynomial-time algorithm (including meta-algorithms that try many polynomial-time strategies) can reliably exploit whatever structure is claimed to exist in order to solve instances efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One commenter proposes 'meta-algorithms' that try many P-time algorithms until one works; a valid P vs NP argument must rule out such possibilities or show that exponentially many algorithmic choices would be required in the worst case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity: be understandable to specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct major proof should be, at minimum, understandable by specialists in the field; ideally the key ideas and structure are comprehensible to those experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments list 'best case' as a proof that is both correct and understandable; long or opaque arguments slow community verification and acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain civil, professional community discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Community responses should focus on technical critique; personal attacks or ad hominem commentary (on age, origin, employment, family) are inappropriate and undermine constructive evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters deplore personal attacks on the author and urge respectful treatment; maintaining civil norms helps productive review and retains community trust.
